questions.q: Amit is the project manager of a software project to create a mobile application that is scheduled to be completed in four months. The project charter is signed and Amit is working now to collect requirements from project stakeholders. The customer requested that the design of the project should be completed after one month. In which document should this condition be documented? *

o.t: Requirements traceability matrix.
Assumptions log.
Scope management plan.
Requirements management plan.

questions.e: The customer's request that the design be completed after one month is a condition or expectation that might impact planning, but it has not yet been analyzed for feasibility or formally accepted into the baseline. Therefore, it should be treated as an assumption or constraint and recorded in the assumptions log. The other options: A. Requirements traceability matrix: This is used to link requirements to project objectives and track them throughout the project life cycle—not for documenting time-bound conditions or assumptions. C. Scope management plan: This outlines how the scope will be defined, validated, and controlled—not for documenting specific stakeholder time constraints. D. Requirements management plan: This defines how requirements will be analyzed, documented, and managed—not where assumptions or stakeholder conditions are noted.

questions.q: A project manager was asked to lead a project of a flight booking website development. The airline requested that the website should be able to support one thousand visitors per hour. This condition is also known as a(n): (choose two) *

o.t: Requirement
Scope
Acceptance criterion
Deliverable

questions.e: Requirement: The system’s ability to support 1000 visitors is a non-functional requirement. Acceptance Criterion: It defines how stakeholders will judge whether the deliverable meets expectations.

questions.q: A project team has identified a number of defects with some deliverables and intends to resolve these as soon as possible. The project manager will need to submit a change request to the change control board (CCB). What should the project manager do before the request is submitted? *

o.t: Implement the changes immediately due to time constraints.
Send the change request to the client for approval.
Complete an impact analysis of each requested change.
Send the change requests to the sponsor for approval.

questions.e: Before submitting a change request, the project manager should analyze the impact on scope, schedule, cost, and other project constraints. This ensures informed decision-making by the CCB.

questions.q: Astral Bank is well-known for offering excellent online services to its customers. As part of their new project, customers will be able to electronically submit a loan request. Three weeks into project execution, the project manager discovers that an important resource has been over-allocated. This project is in need of: *

o.t: Resource leveling
Resource smoothing
Resource calendar
Resource loading

questions.e: Resource leveling adjusts the schedule based on resource constraints. It may delay tasks to resolve over-allocations.

questions.q: In order to ensure that the project is performed in accordance with the organization’s requirements, the project manager carries out a tailoring process. Under this context, Tailoring is: *

o.t: The knowledge and practices which are applicable to most projects in most cases
The application of a set of knowledge, skills, tools, and techniques to the project activities in order to meet its requirements
The selection of the appropriate processes, inputs, tools, techniques, and life cycle phases for managing a project
The application of knowledge, skills, tools, and techniques needed for meeting a program's requirements

questions.e: Tailoring involves choosing the most suitable elements from the PM framework to fit the project needs.t.

questions.q: Network diagrams are a visual display of project work as they show the connection between work activities and how they progress from the project's start to its completion. The longest path in a network diagram is known as: *

o.t: Critical Path
Critical Chain
Float
Free Float

questions.e: The Critical Path is the longest sequence of activities in a project schedule, determining the shortest time to complete the project.

questions.q: An activity has an Early Start (ES) of day 5, a Late Start (LS) of day 12, an Early Finish (EF) of day 10, and a Late Finish (LF) of day 17. Which of the following statements are correct regarding this activity? (Choose two) *

o.t: The activity is on the critical path
The activity is not on the critical path
The activity has a float
The activity has a lag

questions.e: B. The activity is not on the critical path: The critical path has zero float. Since this activity has a float, it is not on the critical path. C. The activity has a float: Float (or slack) is the amount of time that an activity can be delayed without delaying the project. It is calculated as LS - ES or LF - EF. In this case, the float is 12 - 5 = 7 days, indicating that the activity has a float.

questions.q: The project team includes one carpenter who is only available to work part-time. Since her work is on the critical path, the project’s planned completion date had to be pushed back to align with her availability. The adjustment of the project schedule to handle resource constraints is referred to as: *

o.t: Load Balancing
Resource Loading
Resource Leveling
Resource Smoothing

questions.e: Resource leveling adjusts the schedule based on resource availability, even if it affects the project timeline.

questions.q: The following diagram represents the decomposition of the project deliverables into smaller tasks. What is this diagram called? *

o.t: Affinity diagram
Task list
Product roadmap
Work breakdown structure

questions.e: The diagram shown is a hierarchical decomposition of the total scope of work to accomplish the project objectives and create the deliverables. This is known as a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS).

questions.q: You are a project manager in a large organization. Recently, your organization is facing a financial crisis, and there was a mass layoff for many employees in the organization. Many projects were affected because of this layoff. Your project is one of the affected projects because almost 30% of the project resources were released due to the layoff. To deal with the limited number or resources, you adjust the start and finish dates to balance between the demand and available supply of resources. What is the technique you used? *

o.t: Fast Tracking.
Crashing.
Resource Smoothing.
Resource Leveling.

questions.e: Resource leveling is used when resource availability affects task scheduling. It helps balance demand with limited supply.

questions.q: A project sponsor asks the project manager to begin work on a new initiative without a formally approved project charter. What should the project manager do? *

o.t: Proceed with the project since the sponsor has requested it.
Document project objectives and scope and begin execution immediately.
Inform the sponsor that the project cannot officially start without an approved charter.
Start with a stakeholder analysis while waiting for the charter approval.

questions.e: The Project Charter formally authorizes the project and provides the project manager with authority to use organizational resources. Without an approved charter, the project has no formal backing. Starting execution (A, B, D) without a charter risks misalignment and lack of authority.

questions.q: A project is in the execution phase, and the team has completed 60% of the planned work. However, a variance analysis shows that both costs and schedules are significantly deviating from the original plan. What is the best course of action? *

o.t: Conduct a review of the Cost Baseline and Schedule Baseline to assess the extent of the variance and determine corrective actions.
Continue working as planned since 60% of the work is completed and adjustments may not be necessary.
Submit a change request to update the project baselines to reflect current performance.
Increase resource allocation to speed up progress and get back on track.

questions.e: Since both cost and schedule deviations exist, the best first step is to compare actual progress with the Cost Baseline and Schedule Baseline. Variance analysis helps identify whether delays are caused by resource inefficiencies, underestimated effort, or other factors. Updating baselines (C) should only happen after a thorough impact analysis and change control approval. Adding more resources (D) increases costs and may cause additional inefficiencies (e.g., Brook’s Law).

questions.q: Halfway through a major construction project, the client requests a new structural modification that was not originally included in the approved project scope. This modification would require additional budget and extend the timeline. How should the project manager handle this request? *

o.t: Review the Scope Baseline and initiate a formal change request if the modification is not within the approved scope.
Approve the modification immediately to maintain client satisfaction.
Add the new requirement informally and adjust the schedule accordingly.
Inform the client that no changes can be made once the project has started.

questions.e: The Scope Baseline (Scope Statement, WBS, and WBS Dictionary) defines what is included in the project. If the requested modification is not part of the original scope, it must go through the Change Control Process to assess its impact on cost, schedule, and risk. Approving it informally (B, C) leads to scope creep, budget overruns, and potential project failure. Denying all changes (D) is not always realistic—change management exists to handle such requests effectively.

questions.q: During project execution, the project team discovers that several activities are taking longer than originally estimated, causing a schedule delay. The project sponsor insists that the project must still finish on the original deadline. What should the project manager do first? *

o.t: Perform a schedule variance analysis against the Schedule Baseline and identify possible corrective actions.
Immediately crash the schedule by adding more resources to recover lost time.
Request an immediate baseline update to reflect the new timeline.
Ignore the delay, as the team might naturally catch up later in execution.

questions.e: Before taking action, the project manager must analyze the Schedule Baseline to understand the root cause of the delays. Possible corrective actions include: Fast tracking (rearranging tasks to run in parallel where feasible). Crashing (adding resources, but only if it doesn’t cause inefficiencies). Reassessing dependencies and constraints to optimize workflow. Updating the baseline (C) is inappropriate without a formal change request and impact assessment. Ignoring the delay (D) is risky and may result in a missed deadline.

questions.q: A project manager needs to determine the minimum project duration by identifying the longest sequence of dependent activities. Which scheduling technique should be used? *

o.t: Critical Path Method (CPM)
Resource Leveling
Fast Tracking
Monte Carlo Simulation

questions.e: The Critical Path Method (CPM) identifies the longest path of dependent activities and determines the minimum project duration. Resource Leveling (B) is used to adjust resources, not duration. Fast Tracking (C) overlaps activities but does not find the longest path. Monte Carlo Simulation (D) is a risk-based probability analysis.

questions.q: A project manager is analyzing the critical path for a construction project. The project schedule consists of multiple parallel paths, and some activities have float (slack). However, during execution, an unforeseen delay occurs in a non-critical path activity. The project manager realizes that this delay has now impacted the final project completion date. What is the most likely reason for this impact? *

o.t: The delayed activity had negative float, causing it to become part of the critical path.
The delay consumed all available free float, making it a new critical activity.
The original critical path was incorrectly identified during project planning.
The delay affected a fast-tracked activity, automatically extending the project duration.

questions.q: A project team is nearing completion of a large infrastructure project when they discover that a deliverable does not fully meet the original scope requirements. The project manager realizes that an incorrect assumption was made during the planning phase. What should be the first step? *

o.t: Submit a change request to update the Scope Baseline to reflect the current deliverable.
Assess the variance against the Scope Baseline and determine corrective action.
Accept the deliverable as-is since modifying it at this stage would delay the project.
Ask the project sponsor to approve the incomplete deliverable to close the project on time.

questions.e: Scope variance must be assessed before taking action. If the deliverable does not meet the agreed-upon scope, the team must determine whether corrective actions, rework, or formal change control are required. Modifying the Scope Baseline retroactively (A) without justification violates change control principles. Accepting an incomplete deliverable (C, D) leads to stakeholder dissatisfaction and potential project failure.

questions.q: A project team is experiencing communication breakdowns, and stakeholders are frequently misaligned on expectations. The project manager wants to address this issue using the Project Management Plan. Which specific component should be reviewed first? *

o.t: Stakeholder Engagement Plan
Communications Management Plan
Scope Management Plan
Project Charter

questions.e: The Communications Management Plan defines who needs what information, how it is delivered, and when it is shared. Stakeholder Engagement Plan (A) focuses on stakeholder relationships but does not directly address communication breakdowns. Scope Management Plan (C) defines scope-related processes but is unrelated to communication issues. Project Charter (D) provides high-level project authorization but does not manage communication processes.

questions.q: A project manager is planning a software development project where the testing phase can begin only after 50% of the coding is completed. Which type of dependency and lag should be used to model this relationship? *

o.t: Start-to-Start (SS) with a 50% progress milestone
Finish-to-Finish (FF) with a lead time
Finish-to-Start (FS) with a lag time
Start-to-Finish (SF) with a dependency buffer

questions.e: Start-to-Start (SS) means two activities can start at different times but overlap. Since testing can begin after 50% of coding is complete, it indicates a partial dependency rather than waiting for full completion. Finish-to-Finish (FF) (B) would require both to finish together, which is incorrect. Finish-to-Start (FS) (C) means testing would have to wait for full completion, which is not the case. Start-to-Finish (SF) (D) is an unusual dependency and does not apply here.

questions.q: During the execution phase of a large infrastructure project, a key stakeholder informally requests several minor modifications to the original design. The project manager, wanting to maintain stakeholder satisfaction, instructs the team to implement these changes without documenting them or updating the project plan. Over time, additional unapproved modifications accumulate, increasing project costs and extending the schedule. What should the project manager have done to prevent this situation? *

o.t: Enforce strict adherence to the original scope and reject all change requests.
Implement a formal change control process to assess the impact of all modifications before approval.
Allow minor changes without documentation, but track larger modifications through change control.
Accept only changes that do not affect cost or schedule to maintain project flexibility.

questions.e: Scope creep occurs when uncontrolled changes are made to a project without going through formal change management. A well-defined change control process ensures all modifications are evaluated for cost, schedule, and risk impact before approval. Strictly rejecting all changes (A) may not be realistic in dynamic projects. Allowing undocumented changes (C, D) leads to hidden costs, schedule overruns, and stakeholder misalignment.

questions.q: A project is in the execution phase when a key stakeholder requests a significant change to the project scope. The change would impact the timeline and budget. What is the first step the project manager should take? *

o.t: Implement the change immediately to meet stakeholder expectations.
Refer the request to the Change Control Board (CCB) for approval.
Conduct an impact analysis to evaluate the effect on scope, schedule, and cost.
Reject the change request because it was not part of the original plan.

questions.e: Before escalating a change request to the Change Control Board (CCB), the project manager must assess its impact. Impact analysis helps determine feasibility, risks, and necessary adjustments. Implementing changes without evaluation (A) leads to uncontrolled scope creep. Escalating to the CCB (B) is premature without impact assessment. Rejecting changes outright (D) may not align with business needs.

questions.q: During the execution phase of a Waterfall project, the project sponsor insists on a critical scope change but does not want to adjust the budget or timeline. What is the best approach for the project manager? *

o.t: Accept the change and find ways to deliver within the existing constraints.
Conduct a trade-off analysis and present options, such as reducing other deliverables.
Reject the change since it does not align with the original project scope.
Implement the change and request additional contingency funds later.

questions.e: A trade-off analysis helps evaluate the feasibility of incorporating the change within existing constraints. Changes in Waterfall projects typically require adjustments to cost, schedule, or scope. Blindly accepting the change (A) increases project risks. Outright rejection (C) without presenting alternatives may not be an effective stakeholder management strategy. Implementing first and asking for funds later (D) leads to uncontrolled project cost overruns.

questions.q: A Waterfall project has a detailed project schedule, but a key supplier notifies the team of a late delivery, which will impact critical path activities. What is the best way to handle this situation? *

o.t: Use schedule compression techniques like crashing or fast-tracking.
Extend the project deadline to accommodate the delay.
Replace the supplier immediately with a new vendor.
Ignore the delay, assuming other activities will make up for lost time.

questions.e: Crashing (adding resources) or Fast-Tracking (overlapping activities) are schedule compression techniques used to mitigate delays affecting the critical path. Option B delays project completion. Option C may cause additional risks and costs. Option D assumes without validating, which is poor risk management.

questions.q: A project is near completion when the client requests additional functionality that was not part of the approved scope. The team believes the change is minor and can be implemented without formal approval. What is the best action for the project manager? *

o.t: Implement the change since the team believes it will not impact the schedule.
Document the request and submit it through the formal change control process.
Reject the request because it is too late in the project lifecycle.
Inform the client that additional changes can be addressed in a future project phase.

questions.e: All changes, regardless of size, must go through formal change control in Waterfall projects. Even "minor" changes can have unintended schedule, cost, and quality impacts. Implementing changes without approval (A) risks scope creep. Outright rejection (C) or deferring changes (D) without assessment may not align with stakeholder needs.

questions.q: A project is in the planning phase, and the project manager is creating a detailed Work Breakdown Structure (WBS). Which principle should be followed to ensure the WBS is effective? *

o.t: Break down work into activities and assign specific durations.
Ensure each work package is detailed enough to be estimated and managed effectively.
Include only major deliverables and leave details for later phases.
Structure the WBS based on available resources rather than deliverables.

questions.e: An effective WBS breaks the project into manageable work packages, making it easier to estimate costs, duration, and assign responsibilities. Option A refers to scheduling, not WBS structure. Option C ignores the need for detailed scope definition. Option D should be deliverable-based, not resource-based.
